proposal: This application is to undertake work to 42 highway trees in Newcastle-under-Lyme Town Centre. Work proposals for each tree are listed on the attached tree survey. Tree pruning and felling has been requested to enable CCTV to be fully effective. However, this would result in a sharp deterioration in the landscape quality of the town so this proposal represents a compromise with only one tree to fell and modest pruning of other trees, mainly by way of crown lifting and lateral pruning of branches away from buildings.It is likely that two new cameras will be set up where adequate tree-pruning is deemed to be unfeasible. The tree to fell is a semi-mature honey locust located at the Ironmarket end of Castle Walk. The removal of this one tree will enable unhindered CCTV coverage in Castle Walk. In view of the reason for felling we do not propose to replace this tree with a new specimen. The Staffordshire County Council Senior Tree Officer has been consulted over these proposals and has indicated his support for the proposals.

proposal: T1 Lime Removal. On the grounds that the tree is causing damage to the neighbouring wall and is physically encroaching into a residents garden. These issues raise concerns regarding the protection of neighbouring property, the ongoing impact on the residents enjoyment and use of their garden, and the potential for further damage if the tree is retained. The trees proximity to the boundary and its apparent impact on the neighbouring wall suggest that its continued retention may be causing an unreasonable level of interference with the adjacent property. If the damage is ongoing, retaining the tree could result in further deterioration and increased repair costs. Removal would eliminate the source of the encroachment and allow the affected wall and boundary area to be repaired and maintained without continued interference from the tree. Furthermore, the trees encroachment into a residents garden affects the residents ability to enjoy and use their outdoor space without obstruction. The impact on neighbouring amenity and property should therefore be given due consideration when assessing whether the tree remains suitable for retention in its current location. On balance, removal of T1 Lime should be considered a reasonable and proportionate solution, subject to confirmation of the damage, the extent of the encroachment and an assessment of any alternative management options. Where the damage cannot be adequately resolved through pruning or other arboricultural measures, removal may be the most effective long-term means of preventing further interference with the neighbouring property.
